My personal and HTML-editor opinion is that it would still be nice to use switch as an opportunity to design a new form control element, separate from `<input>`. It could embody modern best practices, avoid the mistakes of `<input>` like `value=""` vs. `defaultValue`, and avoid `HTMLInputElement`'s everything-everywhere-all-at-once design. But, I can understand how that's more work, and has some drawbacks around progressive enhancement etc. So if we go the `<input type=checkbox switch>` route, I will be sad at the missed opportunity, but nothing more.

+1 to perhaps minting a new element for this, rather than further tangling the `<input>` element. But I also agree with @domenic that it would be "ok" to do it this way.

Another potential issue is that there are some strong opinions pushing back on the concept of toggle buttons as a UI element. E.g. [Toggles suck!](https://axesslab.com/toggles-suck/)

Having said that, my main push back against this PR is that I believe that any new element like this needs to be developer-styleable out of the gate. I think we should be standardizing the parts of the control and allowing for e.g. CSS pseudo elements to style the parts, or sub-elements to replace parts of the control if needed. I would push back against a UA-provided switch that isn't easy to customize.

I think switches (and checkboxes) are simple enough that existing techniques might suffice? In particular: `appearance: none` + selectors for `:checked` = style the two states however you like. And I *think* (but am not sure) that existing CSS animations and transitions are enough to allow custom transitions between the states?

This would be a different story if there were developer-controlled content inside the switch/checkbox, like there is with selectmenu or more complex inputs. But the "customizable UI content" of switch/checkbox seems to me to be, what they look like in their two/three states, and transitions between those states.

I agree and disagree all at the same time. If we look at any other major application platform ([iOS](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/uiswitch), [Android](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/views/components/togglebutton), [Windows](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/design/controls/toggles)) they all come with switch and checkbox solutions as separate controls and most of them have more complex content underneath of them. While we "can achieve" a checkbox look how we want I still need to wrap it and then build out my end desired solution when I could, assuming I had access to the parts adjust the border-radius, shadows, etc. 

Because of this I'm going to +1 @mfreed7 recommendation of a new element and having them styleable out of the box.

This is what developers (rightfully) complain about though. Like, change the border style. Change the “on/off” symbols. Change any colors used. Etc.

opinionated/rushed CSS aside - https://codepen.io/scottohara/pen/oNQmraB - it's not a lot of work to restyle using the appearance approach - so i personally don't mind one way or the other (the inclusion of pseudo elements specific to `switch` attribute being added would be very welcome). @domenic and @mfreed7, there is a draft PR for a switch proposal at OpenUI: https://github.com/openui/open-ui/pull/785

Preview: https://deploy-preview-785--open-ui.netlify.app/components/switch.explainer/

For styling, pseudo elements can be added to this proposal. I hope we can get consensus at least on the basic HTML approach before that though.

@nt1m thanks for the feedback. Backwards compatibility would be a nice plus. There are two other aspects that differentiate the switch from a checkbox.

1. Most analysed design systems specify that a switch can't have an indeterminate state and should toggle a binary option only
2. Most analysed design systems encourage to take immediate action upon toggling the switch where checkboxes have to be submitted via form in order to take effect (in most cases). In that regard, the switch behaves more like a stateful button.

After doing this research, I wondered if a switch should even be a form control.

@gfellerph The implementation proposed in this PR already addresses your first point; the data submitted by a switch control is binary only, and it does not have an indeterminate visual state nor does it match the indeterminate pseudo-class. As for the second point, while I agree that switches most commonly take immediate action in UIs, it's still not always the case on the web (nor is it for the real-world switches the control is modeled off of). 

As such, we still want it to be a form control because right now we want that choice between immediate action and form data to be there, and we want it to be easy for web-developers to implement either way.

I'm particularly unkeen on the idea this would default to the same value semantics as checkboxes. "on" being the default checked value and no value being submitted when "unchecked" is fairly unintuitive for a checkbox imo.

It would be even less intuitive for a switch. A switch imo always has a value it's true or false (though an indeterminate null state could also be useful), unlike a checkbox where it could be argued that unchecked is an empty state.

Having a basic backward compat "switch" initially and then adding `<switch>` as something new in future could be okay I guess but would probably be hard to explain to newbies.

beyond appearance, this is about how the control is exposed to assistive technologies, and how they then announce it. one of the confusing aspects of "faking" switch controls with just a checkbox and CSS is that for screen reader users, it's still announced as "checkbox, not checked / checkbox, checked", which depending on the label used can be very confusing

Should `<input type=checkbox switch>` be [barred from constraint validation](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#barred-from-constraint-validation)? I suspect the answer is yes, given the semantic difference between checkboxes and switches.

> beyond appearance, this is about how the control is exposed to assistive technologies, and how they then announce it. one of the confusing aspects of "faking" switch controls with just a checkbox and CSS is that for screen reader users, it's still announced as "checkbox, not checked / checkbox, checked", which depending on the label used can be very confusing

ARIA has [role=switch](https://w3c.github.io/aria/#switch) for this; `<input type=checkbox switch>` is a native HTML way of creating something that gets exposed to AT as an element with `role=switch` would be.
ARIA allows for a switch to be marked as required, so while the semantics for a checkbox/switch do differ, since it can be marked as required it should thus allow for it to be validated.

I think a new switch control should be `appearance: none` in the UA stylesheet and have defined default styles (using accent-color) which developers can tweak in author CSS, probably with pseudo-elements.
That would not work for Apple platforms. We want the switch to have an appearance that matches the established platform conventions, similar to existing form controls.

> I think a new switch control should be `appearance: none` in the UA stylesheet and have defined default styles (using accent-color) which developers can tweak in author CSS, probably with pseudo-elements.

I'm very much in favor of the second part of this sentence - with `appearance:none`, the switch should have a defined (standardized) set of styles which can be developer-tweaked via CSS. I'm agnostic to whether the *default* value of `appearance` is `none` for this control. It could be `auto`.

> That would not work for Apple platforms. We want the switch to have an appearance that matches the established platform conventions, similar to existing form controls.

@emilio my intuition would be that it should render just like `<input type=checkbox>` (with `appearance:auto`), with a different look and feel. (I thought all form controls were replaced elements.)

I think we should tackle the pseudo-elements separately in a follow-up, but ideally they work the same way as they do on `<input type=range>` and other controls. If using them there turns `appearance:auto` into `appearance:none` for instance, `<input type=checkbox switch>` should do the same. Making them work for `appearance:none` seems straightforward. `appearance:bikeshed` is the more challenging endeavor.

@annevk well part of the different look and feel also implies different size and different baseline presumably (checkboxes are squares, this presumably will be rectangular?).

> I thought all form controls were replaced elements.

Kind of? There are more complicated form controls, because pseudo-elements, that quack as replaced but still need more complex definitions. In particular, need to either:

 * Define what properties apply to the various pseudo-elements (presumably not allowing properties that expose the underlying layout model).
 * Define that layout model. I _think_ if we define that the switch uses block layout internally that should be reasonably flexible and easy to implement across browsers.
 * Define that switch is not replaced and honors `display`. This is probably more flexible, but more unlike other form controls.

> I think we should tackle the pseudo-elements separately in a follow-up, but ideally they work the same way as they do on `<input type=range>` and other controls.

Well, part of this whole issue is that those pseudo-elements aren't quite interoperable today.

For example there are [multiple things you can't do to the thumb in Gecko](https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/rev/077fc34d03b85b09add26b5f99f1a3a3a72c8720/layout/style/res/forms.css#827,833-838) because of all this "layout model not being defined" thing.

It seems WebKit uses `RenderSlider` (which [is a flexbox](https://searchfox.org/wubkat/rev/4202a8a96888091029f0538738502352b878041b/Source/WebCore/rendering/RenderSlider.h#30)) for `<input type=range>`, while Blink uses a generic flexbox but [wants to get rid of it](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1131352)).

It also seems that Blink doesn't create a replaced box for a bunch of input types. E.g, `<input type=date>` and co seem to just honor `display` unless I'm missing something ([code](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/renderer/core/html/forms/input_type_view.cc;l=97-104;drc=b74163d3d63e781ce9899ec6a4e5a7c113d960b9)). So maybe making `<input type=switch>` do so isn't so terrible.

But in any case, this is a huge mess, and I don't really want to add to that mess for new things. We should define what approach to take here. Implementation wise I think either approach is fine.
I wonder if some of the layout folks in Blink / WebKit would have opinions on the above. cc @bfgeek @smfr @dholbert

> @mfreed7 can Chromium be considered supportive provided we continue to jointly seek a solution around `appearance:base` that works for all form controls?

I'd be hesitant to want to ship a new switch element that depends (for stylability) on a new thing that might or might not come later. What if we decide that `appearance:none` switches should be stylable and interoperable? That might not be web compatible if we ship it before figuring out the stylability question. Generally, I don't think we should introduce any new form controls that aren't stylable by default.

To be clear, I am generally supportive of introducing a "switch" input. I just want it to be complete before we land it.

I am also generally supportive of working toward an `appearance` behavior that provides:

1. A mode that is visually-interoperable among browsers.
2. A mode (perhaps same as 1) that is fully* stylable.
3. A mode (which can be optional) that is UA-styled and proprietary.

*I define "fully stylable" to mean >90% of common styling use cases are achievable.

> @mfreed7 Styling doesn't need to be blocked on appearance: base. What's blocked on appearance: base would rather be the UA styles of the different pseudos + control itself. The UA can always provide 0x0 pseudo elements that are styleable when appearance: none is used.

That's true, assuming the "pseudos + control itself" part is defined. I don't believe this PR contains any anatomy for the control, does it? Apologies if it has been added and I didn't see it.

> If you think that is a still an issue, we can always try to define basic UA styles for appearance: none (like text inputs do) but it would be inconsistent with checkboxes/radios, and doesn't give authors the possibility to style from scratch.
>
> Putting UA styles on appearance: base is a win, since authors would be able to start from basic styling and also choose to start from scratch (appearance: none).

Let's discuss `appearance:none` and `appearance:base` over on https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/5998, if that's ok with you.

> That's true, assuming the "pseudos + control itself" part is defined. I don't believe this PR contains any anatomy for the control, does it? Apologies if it has been added and I didn't see it.

I think it's out of scope for WHATWG? This should be part of the CSSWG spec.

> > That's true, assuming the "pseudos + control itself" part is defined. I don't believe this PR contains any anatomy for the control, does it? Apologies if it has been added and I didn't see it.
> 
> I think it's out of scope for WHATWG? This should be part of the CSSWG spec.

I guess it depends? Certainly CSSWG needs to discuss which pseudos to add, and what they mean in words. But then HTML needs to connect them to real parts of a real control, including the structure of those parts. The switch component is quite similar to the `<input type=range>` control, and might share some parts. But the actual structure matters. E.g. is the `::thumb` element a sibling of the `::track` or a child? See https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/4410#issuecomment-1722028412 for very similar questions - note that the answers to those questions likely need to be defined in HTML/DOM, since they're about the structure of the DOM.
From Mozilla's POV we're directionally supportive but the pseudo-elements and styling details need to be defined.

As harm reduction, it probably makes sense to add something like this, but I think the spec needs more detail to ensure implementations actually reduce the [harm from overuse of switch elements](https://axesslab.com/toggles-suck/). For example: * Should the '[inline-start](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-writing-modes-3/#inline-start)' edge be "off" and the '[inline-end](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-writing-modes-3/#inline-end)' edge be "on"? Or 'left' and 'right'? This is semantic, not just style, because it determines whether `

Off On

` is correct. * Should all implementations default to showing some text inside the control, or is it sufficient for https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/use-of-color.html to allow users to turn on an OS setting that shows the setting in a non-color way? * Is there any guidance for what that text should be? Do non-tech users understand that "O" is off and "I" is on? * Can HTML say anything about when the semantics of a situation make it appropriate to use a switch instead of a checkbox? >Can we use this attribute on buttons? Switches are toggle buttons after all. I really wish we had a `<switch>` element instead.

well, sort of.  There _is_ a concept of a toggle button which can be created by use of `aria-pressed` on a button element, but that is "different" than a switch. Probably a new issue/proposal to file, rather than something this effort should tackle.

The Chrome DOM team doesn't think the switch implementation in Safari is ready to ship, but Safari has [announced that it's shipping in 17.4](https://webkit.org/blog/15054/an-html-switch-control/). While browsers can always make conscious decisions to ship unilaterally, we should always _try_ to reach consensus first, but we don’t have that yet and I’m not sure it was requested explicitly (and if it was we would have said that it is on a reasonable track but is not yet done). This PR is under active design, and has open questions such as a lack of an interoperable rendering model, or support for customizable styling. There is also an [explainer at OpenUI](https://open-ui.org/components/switch.explainer/) which has useful aspects not already incorporated here.

We also believe it is a [mistake](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/9546#issuecomment-1660741288) to add another un-styleable form control (we don’t think `appearance:none` is good enough) to the platform, since styleability is a core reason why developers fail to adopt the built-in controls. Work is underway to add styleability to other existing form controls, but doing so without breaking web compat is challenging, and may end up causing pain for web developers during the migration.

Finally, the feature isn't specified well enough to ship. Especially until the track and thumb are customizable, authors need to know and possibly control which side of the element is on vs off. Also, as @scottaohara [noticed last week](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/9546#issuecomment-1974015259), that semantic difference probably includes labels for the two states, but the design that Safari's shipping doesn't address that aspect and may foreclose the possibility of using nested elements to define those labels. Implementers also need to know how to make the visual appearance accessible. 

We also want to emphasize that this comment doesn't reflect negatively on the quality of @lilyspiniolas' proposal, specification, or implementation to date. It's about how to proceed since then.

Listeners for `pointerdown` and `pointermove` run mid-drag, so script can set `checked`, remove `switch`, change `type`, or disable the control.
